items.title: 8.15 Effect of a catalyst on equilibrium

source_refs.note: Topic 8.15, printed page 182 (Figure 8.3, carried by the Le Chatelier original).

blocks.title: Catalyst
blocks.text: A catalyst is a substance which increases the rate of a chemical reaction without itself being consumed. It does not change the equilibrium position or the equilibrium constant of a reaction; it speeds up the rate at which equilibrium is attained, so the yield of the reaction stays the same.

blocks.alt: An energy profile for a reversible reaction. The uncatalysed path (blue) has a high activated state, the catalysed path (red) a lower one. Double arrows mark Ea uncatalysed and Ea' catalysed, and delta H between reactants and products is unchanged. A note says both forward and reverse barriers fall, so equilibrium comes sooner but its position does not change.
blocks.caption: Effect of a catalyst on reversible reactions (original diagram after Figure 8.3).

blocks.text: A catalyst provides a new path of lower activation energy. On a graph of potential energy against reaction coordinate the maximum of the curve is lower in the presence of a catalyst: the activation energy of the uncatalysed reaction, Ea, is replaced by a smaller Ea' for the catalysed one, for both the forward and the reverse reaction, while the energies of reactants and products, and so delta H, are unchanged.
